newsitem.title: USA: California floods cause havoc in Yosemite Park.
newsitem.headline: California floods cause havoc in Yosemite Park.

text.p: Floods have washed away roads and damaged bridges and cabins in Yosemite National Park in California, closing the park for at least the rest of this month, officials said on Wednesday.

The majestic park in the Sierra Nevada, a natural marvel, was one of the places where the forces of nature were unleashed most violently during the storms and floods that hit California last week, as if they were trying to reclaim the park from human civilisation.
"We are amazed and thrilled by the power of nature," park spokeswoman Ginger Burley said.

Only one road out of the park -- Highway 41 -- has been reopened, for use in daylight hours by employees. The park will remain closed to visitors through the end of January and perhaps beyond, Burley said.
About 900 tourists, stranded at Yosemite for two days by floods, were evacuated last week and 500 park employees were evacuated on Tuesday, leaving about 500 still there.
Officials were still assessing the damage and there was no estimate of how much it would cost to repair even if they decided to replace all of the damaged facilities.

The 760,000-acre (307,000-hectare) park, 150 miles (240 kms) southeast of San Francisco, is visited by four million hikers, climbers and sightseers each year, drawn by its towering mountains, high waterfalls and scenic wilderness.
The Merced River overflowed its banks, sending fast-moving water streaming through parking lots and campgrounds and cutting off roads.

The floods knocked out a 200-yard (metre) section of road and the sewer line that ran under it, disabling the sewer system in Yosemite Valley, where the park's headquarters and lodging are located and where many park employees live.
The section of road was washed away so completely "you can't even tell there was ever a road there," Burley said.
The storm brought rocks and trees crashing down and the floods, the worst to hit the park in 40 years, caused water well pumps to fail.
"The river came up and spread out, it was a gigantic lake. Things floated around, picnic tables are on top of rocks, pieces of road are washed away," Burley said.
The flood washed away part of the pavement from one bridge, leaving just stone pillars and steel beams. Campgrounds on the flood plain looked like big sandy beaches, she said.
Some guest cabins suffered water damage and some were washed off their foundations. Some larger buildings had water inside too, Burley said.
Park officials now had to decide whether to rebuild facilities on the flood plain. "Those are decisions that won't be taken right away," Burley said.
For now workers were concentrating on trying to repair the broken sewer line, she said. It would be many months before repairs were completed, she said.

Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks, in the Sierra Nevada south of Yosemite, were not as badly damaged by the floods and were open to the public, officials said. "Compared to the damage sustained in other places we do feel fortunate," park spokeswoman Malinee Crapsey said.
A portion of highway was washed away in Sequoia National Park and in another area mud and rock covered the road.
But the most badly damaged areas were parts of the park that are always closed in the winter, she said. "While there is damage, it's not affecting public access," Crapsey said.
